tips.title: A and B are codominant; O is recessive
tips.body: **Codominant** means **both are expressed** when present together, so `AB` gives blood group **AB** — not one masking the other. **O** is recessive, so group O requires **OO**. Three alleles for one gene is what "multiple alleles" means.

tips.title: Males have only one X
tips.body: A sex-linked allele sits on the **X** chromosome. A male is **XY**, so he has **only one X** and **no second copy to mask a recessive allele** — one copy is enough to be affected. That single fact explains the whole topic.

tips.title: Codominant is not the same as incomplete
tips.body: **Codominant** means **both alleles are fully expressed** — an `AB` person has **both** A and B antigens, not a blend. Do not describe it as a mixture or an intermediate.

tips.title: Write sex-linked genotypes on the chromosomes
tips.body: Write **XᴺXⁿ** and **XⁿY**, not `Nn` and `n`. Putting the allele **on the X** is what makes the diagram work, and it shows the examiner you understand why males are affected more often.

tips.title: Percentages of all children, or of sons?
tips.body: A carrier mother and unaffected father give **25%** affected among **all children**, but **50%** among the **sons**. Read which the question asks for — the two answers are both correct for different questions.

why.matters:
The genetics in the last topic stops being abstract here. A one-in-four chance is a number on a page until it is a family deciding what to do about it.

So this topic is half biology and half something harder: what a test can and cannot tell you, what a **probability** means for one family rather than for a thousand, and why people who agree on every fact can reach opposite decisions. For the Human Genome Project, the command word is **discuss**: applications and concerns, both.

examples.title: Why cystic fibrosis skips generations and Huntington's does not
examples.body:
Cystic fibrosis is **recessive**: two copies are needed, so a person with one is a carrier who never knows. The allele travels quietly for generations and appears when two carriers have a child.

Huntington's disease is **dominant**: one copy is enough, so anybody who has the allele will develop the condition, and it can be traced straight down a family tree. The difference is not the severity — it is how many copies it takes, and that decides everything about how the condition moves through a family.

visual.alt: A table contrasting cystic fibrosis, a recessive condition needing two copies so that carriers are unaware and it can skip generations, with Huntington's disease, a dominant condition needing one copy and appearing in every generation

examples.title: What a screening result actually tells you
examples.body:
A screening test does not usually answer *does this child have the condition*. It answers *how likely is it*, and the difference matters enormously to the family holding the result.

A test can also be wrong in two directions. A **false positive** causes distress and may lead to a further test that carries its own risk; a **false negative** gives false reassurance. Neither is a failure of the biology — every test has them — and any sensible discussion of screening has to include both.

visual.alt: A table of the four outcomes of a screening test: a positive or negative result that is right or wrong, with what each means for the family, including the distress of a false positive and the false reassurance of a false negative

examples.title: Why two families decide differently
examples.body:
Given the same test, the same odds and the same condition, people reach opposite conclusions — and neither is making a mistake about the biology.

The arguments are not scientific ones. They are about what a life with a condition is like, what the family can manage, what the risk of the test itself is worth, and beliefs that nothing in this course addresses. That is why a good answer about testing gives **both sides** before reaching any conclusion: one that recommends without the other side has left half of it out.

boxes.title: Against
boxes.body: The test can carry a risk of its own.

boxes.title: For
boxes.body: A negative result removes years of worry.

steps.title: Codominance and multiple alleles
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **Most examples of inheritance use two alleles, one dominant and one recessive. The ABO blood group system is more complicated, and the specification asks for it specifically.**

**Multiple alleles.** The gene for blood group has **three** alleles in the population — **A**, **B** and **O** — although any one person still has only **two** of them, one from each parent. That is what "multiple alleles" means: more than two versions exist, not that one person has more than two.

**Codominance.** **A and B are codominant**, which means that when both are present **both are fully expressed**. A person with genotype `AB` has blood group **AB**, with **both** A and B antigens on their red blood cells.

**This is not a blend.** Codominance is often described wrongly as a mixture or an in-between. Both alleles are expressed **completely and separately** — the person has both antigens, not an average of them.

**O is recessive** to both A and B. So group O requires **two O alleles**, `OO`.

**The genotypes and the groups they give:**

- `AA` or `AO` → group **A**
- `BB` or `BO` → group **B**
- `AB` → group **AB**
- `OO` → group **O**

**Notice the consequence.** Someone with group A may be `AA` **or** `AO`, so they may be carrying an O allele without showing it — which is why two group A parents can have a group O child.

steps.title: Sex-linked inheritance
steps.body:
*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **A sex-linked gene is one carried on a sex chromosome**, and in practice this means the **X** chromosome, which is much larger than the Y and carries many more genes.

**The key fact, from which everything else follows:** a **female is XX** and so has **two** copies of every X-linked gene, but a **male is XY** and has **only one**.

**What that means for a recessive allele.** In a **female**, a recessive allele on one X can be **masked** by a normal allele on the other — she is a **carrier**, with the allele but not the condition. In a **male**, there is **no second X to mask it**, so a **single** recessive allele is **expressed** and he is affected.

**So sex-linked recessive conditions are far more common in males** — and that is the observation these questions test.

**Writing the genotypes.** Put the allele **on the chromosome**: **XᴺXᴺ** for an unaffected female, **XᴺXⁿ** for a carrier female, **XⁿXⁿ** for an affected female, and **XᴺY** or **XⁿY** for males. Writing `Nn` alone loses the whole point.

**Notice there is no carrier male.** A male either has the allele and is **affected**, or does not have it at all. Only females can carry without showing.

**A worked cross.** A **carrier mother (XᴺXⁿ)** and an **unaffected father (XᴺY)** give four equally likely children: **XᴺXᴺ**, **XᴺXⁿ**, **XᴺY** and **XⁿY**.

So: one unaffected daughter, one **carrier** daughter, one unaffected son, and one **affected** son. That is **25% of all children** affected — but **50% of the sons**, and **no daughters at all**.

**Read the question carefully**, because both of those percentages are correct answers to different questions.

**A son never inherits an X-linked allele from his father.** A son receives his father's **Y**; his only X comes from his mother. So an **affected father (XⁿY)** and a **non-carrier mother (XᴺXᴺ)** have **no affected sons**, but **every daughter** receives his Xⁿ and is a **carrier**.

**Examples.** Red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are both sex-linked recessive disorders.

steps.title: The Human Genome Project
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to discuss the outcomes of the Human Genome Project and its potential applications within medicine.**

**What it was.** An international effort to determine the **complete sequence of bases in human DNA** — the entire human **genome**, which is the **entire DNA of an organism**. It required collaboration between scientists in many countries over many years.

**The outcomes.** It produced a **complete reference sequence** of human DNA, identified the **locations of genes**, and revealed that humans have far **fewer genes** than had been expected. It also showed how **similar** any two human genomes are, and made the data **publicly available** to researchers everywhere.

**Potential applications within medicine:**

**Predicting risk of disease.** Knowing which variants are associated with a condition allows a person's risk to be estimated, so that monitoring or prevention can begin early.

**Improved diagnosis.** A genetic test can confirm a diagnosis that would otherwise be uncertain, or identify which of several similar conditions someone has.

**Personalised medicine.** People respond differently to the same drug because of genetic differences. Knowing a patient's genome allows the **drug and dose** to be chosen to suit them, improving effectiveness and reducing side effects.

**New treatments.** Identifying the gene responsible for a condition is the first step towards developing a treatment that targets the cause.

**Tracing human ancestry**, and studying how populations have migrated and are related.

**Concerns worth raising**, since the specification says **discuss**. Genetic information is extremely **personal**, and there are questions about who may see it — insurers or employers might use it to discriminate. Being told of a risk for a condition with **no available treatment** may cause distress without benefit. And a raised risk is a **probability**, not a certainty, which is easily misunderstood.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **Define codominance as both alleles being fully expressed.** An `AB` individual has **both** A and B antigens. Describing it as a blend, a mixture or an intermediate is wrong and is penalised — codominance is not the same as an average.

*(Biology only.)* **Explain multiple alleles precisely.** **Three** alleles exist **in the population**, but any **one person has two**, one from each parent. Answers implying an individual carries all three are common.

*(Biology only.)* **Remember that group A hides an O.** Someone of group A may be `AA` **or** `AO`. That is why **two group A parents can have a group O child** — both must be `AO`, and each passes on the O.

*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **Build every sex-linked answer on the one X.** A male is **XY**, so he has **only one X** and therefore **no second allele to mask a recessive one**. A single copy is enough. A female has **two**, so she can carry without showing. Every other fact in the topic follows from this.

*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **Write the genotypes on the chromosomes**: **XᴺXⁿ**, **XⁿY**. Writing `Nn` or `n` loses the structure that makes the explanation work, and examiners look for it.

*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **Note there is no such thing as a carrier male.** He either has the allele and is **affected**, or does not have it. Only females carry.

*(Higher tier, Biology only.)* **Read which percentage is wanted.** A carrier mother and unaffected father give **25%** of **all children** affected but **50%** of the **sons** — and **no affected daughters**. Both figures are right, for different questions.

**Discuss the Human Genome Project, do not just list.** Give the medical applications — **risk prediction**, **diagnosis**, **personalised medicine**, **new treatments** — and then the concerns: **privacy** and possible discrimination by insurers or employers, the distress of learning about an **untreatable** risk, and the fact that a raised risk is a **probability** rather than a certainty. The command word is *discuss*, so both sides are expected.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The ABO gene has **three alleles** in the population: **A**, **B** and **O** — but **two per person**.
- **A and B are codominant**: when both are present, **both are fully expressed**.
- **O is recessive**, so group O requires **OO**.
- `AA` or `AO` → **A**; `BB` or `BO` → **B**; `AB` → **AB**; `OO` → **O**.
- A group A person may be `AO`, **carrying an O allele** without showing it.
- `AO × BO` gives **all four blood groups**, each with a **25%** chance.
- A **sex-linked** gene is carried on the **X** chromosome.
- A **female is XX** and has **two** copies; a **male is XY** and has **only one**.
- A male has **no second X to mask a recessive allele**, so **one copy** makes him affected.
- So sex-linked recessive conditions are **far more common in males**.
- Females can be **carriers**; there is **no carrier male**.
- Write genotypes on the chromosome: **XᴺXⁿ**, **XⁿY**.
- A carrier mother and unaffected father: **25%** of children, **50%** of sons, **no daughters** affected.
- An affected father and non-carrier mother: **every daughter a carrier**, **no son affected**, because sons get his Y.
- The **Human Genome Project** sequenced the **entire human genome**.
- Applications: **risk prediction**, **diagnosis**, **personalised medicine**, **new treatments** — with concerns about **privacy** and discrimination.

questions.prompt: Explain why sex-linked recessive conditions are more common in males than in females, using a genetic diagram for a carrier mother and an unaffected father.
questions.solution:
A **sex-linked** gene is one carried on a **sex chromosome** — in practice the **X** chromosome, which is much larger than the Y and carries many more genes.

**The crucial difference is in the number of copies.** A **female is XX**, so she has **two** copies of every gene on the X chromosome. A **male is XY**, and because the Y chromosome is small and carries different genes, he has **only one copy** of most X-linked genes.

**Why this matters for a recessive allele.** A recessive allele is expressed **only when there is no dominant allele to mask it**.

In a **female**, a recessive allele on one X can be masked by a **normal allele on her other X**. She has the allele but does not have the condition — she is a **carrier**. For a female to be affected she would need the recessive allele on **both** X chromosomes, which is much rarer.

In a **male**, there is **no second X**. Whatever allele is on his single X is **expressed**, because there is nothing to mask it. A **single** recessive allele is therefore enough to make him affected.

This also means there is **no such thing as a carrier male**: he either has the allele and is **affected**, or he does not have it at all.

**A worked cross.** Take a **carrier mother, XᴺXⁿ**, and an **unaffected father, XᴺY**, where N is the normal allele and n the recessive one.

The mother produces gametes carrying **Xᴺ** or **Xⁿ**. The father produces gametes carrying **Xᴺ** or **Y**.

|  | **Xᴺ** | **Y** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Xᴺ** | XᴺXᴺ | XᴺY |
| **Xⁿ** | XᴺXⁿ | XⁿY |

The four equally likely outcomes are:

- **XᴺXᴺ** — an unaffected daughter
- **XᴺXⁿ** — a **carrier** daughter, with the allele but not the condition
- **XᴺY** — an unaffected son
- **XⁿY** — an **affected** son

**So one child in four is affected — 25% of all the children — but that one is a son.** Considering the **sons alone**, one of the two is affected, which is **50% of sons**. **No daughters are affected at all**, since every daughter receives a normal Xᴺ from her father.

Both percentages are correct answers to different questions, so it is essential to read whether the question asks about **all children** or **the sons**.

This cross shows in miniature why the condition is commoner in males: the daughters who inherit the recessive allele become **carriers**, while the sons who inherit it are **affected**.

questions.prompt: Discuss the outcomes of the Human Genome Project and its potential applications within medicine.
questions.solution:
**The Human Genome Project** was an international collaboration to determine the **complete sequence of bases in human DNA** — the entire human **genome**, which is the **entire DNA of an organism**. It took many years and required scientists in many countries to work together and share results.

**Its outcomes** included a **complete reference sequence** of human DNA, the identification of **where genes are located** along the chromosomes, and the finding that humans have considerably **fewer genes** than had been expected. It also showed how **similar** any two human genomes are to one another. The data was made **publicly available**, so that researchers anywhere could build on it — which has arguably mattered as much as the sequence itself.

**Potential applications within medicine** follow from knowing which genes are where and what variants exist.

**Predicting the risk of disease.** Where particular variants are associated with a condition, an individual's risk can be estimated. That allows **earlier monitoring**, lifestyle changes, or preventive treatment before symptoms appear.

**Improved diagnosis.** A genetic test can confirm a diagnosis that would otherwise be uncertain, and can distinguish between conditions with similar symptoms but different causes — which matters because they may need different treatments.

**Personalised medicine.** People **metabolise and respond to drugs differently** because of genetic variation, which is why a drug that works well for one patient may be ineffective or produce severe side effects in another. Knowing a patient's genome allows the **drug and the dose** to be chosen to suit them.

**Developing new treatments.** Identifying the gene responsible for a condition is the first step towards a treatment that targets the **cause** rather than the symptoms.

**Tracing ancestry and population history**, though this is not a medical application.

**The concerns are real, and the command word is *discuss*, so they belong in the answer.**

**Privacy** is the largest. Genetic information is deeply personal, and it says things not only about the individual but about their **relatives**, who never consented. There are serious questions about who may access it — **insurers** might raise premiums or refuse cover, and **employers** might discriminate, on the basis of a risk that may never materialise.

**Psychological harm** is a second concern. Being told of a raised risk for a condition with **no available treatment** may cause lasting distress with nothing that can be done about it. Some people reasonably choose **not** to be tested for this reason.

**Misunderstanding risk** is a third. A raised genetic risk is a **probability**, not a diagnosis or a certainty. Someone may have a variant and never develop the condition, or lack it and develop the condition anyway, since **most phenotypic features result from multiple genes** and from the environment as well.

**On balance**, the project has been enormously valuable — it underpins a great deal of modern medical research, and personalised medicine in particular is only possible because of it. But the benefits depend on the information being handled carefully, and the ethical questions about **who sees genetic data** have not been settled as quickly as the science has advanced.

questions.prompt: A sex-linked recessive condition is caused by an allele on the X chromosome. A man who has the condition (XⁿY) has children with a woman who does not carry the allele (XᴺXᴺ). What percentage of their daughters are expected to be carriers?
questions.solution: The mother can only pass on **Xᴺ**. The father passes **Xⁿ** to every daughter and **Y** to every son. So every daughter is **XᴺXⁿ**, a carrier: **100%**. Every son is **XᴺY** and unaffected, because a son receives his father's Y, never his X.

markScheme.description: mother gives Xᴺ only; father gives Xⁿ or Y
daughters all XᴺXⁿ, sons all XᴺY

questions.prompt: In the ABO blood group system, A and B are codominant and O is recessive to both. A parent with genotype AB has a child with a parent whose genotype is OO. What is the percentage chance that the child has blood group A?
questions.solution: The AB parent gives **A** or **B**; the OO parent can only give **O**. The square holds **AO, AO, BO, BO**, so 2 in 4 children are AO, which is group **A**: **50%**. The other half are group B. None can be group AB or group O, although those are the parents' own groups.

examTechnique.body:
Define **codominance** as **both alleles fully expressed** — never a blend. Remember **three ABO alleles in the population, two per person**, and that group A may be `AA` or `AO`.

Build sex-linked answers on the **single X** in males, and write genotypes **on the chromosome** as XᴺXⁿ. Check whether a percentage is asked of **all children** or of the **sons**.
examinerErrors: Describing codominance as blending or an intermediate.
Implying one person carries all three ABO alleles.
Saying two group A parents cannot have a group O child.
Writing sex-linked genotypes as Nn instead of on the X.
Giving the percentage of sons when asked about all children.
Listing HGP applications without discussing any concerns.
Treating a raised genetic risk as a certainty.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer defines **codominance** as **both alleles fully expressed**, and can say why two group A parents may have a group O child — both are `AO`. It builds every sex-linked explanation on the fact that a male has **only one X**, so there is **nothing to mask** a recessive allele, and concludes correctly that **carrier males do not exist**. It writes genotypes **on the chromosome**, and it reads carefully whether a percentage is of **all children** (25%) or of the **sons** (50%). On the Human Genome Project it **discusses** rather than lists — giving applications **and** the privacy, distress and probability concerns.
